issues.legal_issue: A public authority acting as a landlord remains subject to constitutional requirements of fairness and reasonableness even when its property is exempt from rent-control legislation.
material_facts: The port trust was an instrumentality of the State and leased land to numerous tenants.
The trust undertook a professional valuation exercise after concerns that rents were inadequate to meet maintenance costs and its public duties.
The initial proposed rent increases were many times higher than the rents then being paid.
The trust later offered revised compromise terms, and the court assessed its conduct and proposed rents against the constitutional requirement of fairness.
issues.conclusion: The trust was not free to charge rent as it pleased merely because rent-control legislation did not apply. It could revise rents to address inflation, maintenance, taxes, administration costs and public needs, but could not indulge in rack-renting, profiteering or arbitrary dealings. Its valuation process was not itself improper, although the sudden and exorbitant increases resulting from the initial proposal could not be accepted as such.
issues.legal_principle: Article 14 governs the actions of the State and its instrumentalities, including their contractual conduct as landlords. Exemption from rent-control legislation does not free a public landlord from constitutional review, nor does it subject the landlord indirectly to the same restrictions as the exempted legislation. The court relied on M/s Dwarkadas Marfatia and Sons v. Board of Trustees of the Port of Bombay, Baburao Shantaram More v. Bombay Housing Board, Kumari Shrilekha Vidyarthi v. State of U.P., P.J. Irani v. State of Madras, Rampratap Jaidayal v. Dominion of India, and Ratti Palonji Kapadia v. State of Maharashtra.

predicates.public_authority_landlord_dispute: The proceeding concerns a dispute over the conduct of a public authority acting as a landlord.
predicates.public_authority_acts_as_landlord: The public authority leases property and takes action concerning rent or the tenancy.
predicates.rent_control_exemption_applies: The property or landlord is exempt from the otherwise applicable rent-control restrictions.

issues.definition: When a public authority is challenged in a landlord dispute and its property is exempt from rent control, it must still deal fairly and reasonably with its tenants.

issues.legal_issue: A public landlord’s rent-revision terms may be resolved by reasonable, generally applicable revised proposals, while allowing individual tenants to seek relief for material distinguishing circumstances.
material_facts: The trust’s compromise proposals were considered in proceedings in which the affected lessees had been notified and permitted to participate.
The proposals used the consultants’ valuation work as their basis and prescribed common terms for different categories of leases.

The lessees agreed to lower rates of return for the disputed period than those directed by the High Court, while the trust had previously accepted the compromise proposals as the basis for resolving the dispute.
Some tenants, including a tenant whose land was crossed by an underground storm-water drain, claimed that individual characteristics justified further relief.
The Maharashtra Rent Control Act issue was left open because the record was inadequate to decide it.
issues.conclusion: The compromise proposals were upheld as fair, just and reasonable, with rent revision for the period from 1 April 1994 to 31 March 2000 modified to use rates of return of 10% for non-residential use and 8% for residential use, based on the consultants’ report. The earlier period remained governed by the compromise proposals, and arrears for the later period carried 6% annual interest. The modified terms bound the lessees covered by the representative proceedings, while tenants could seek relief for real and material distinguishing features before a sole adjudicator. The applicability of the later rent-control statute was left open.
issues.legal_principle: Public-authority rent revision must be fair and reasonable under Article 14, and the court may resolve a class-wide dispute on the basis of reasonable common terms while providing a means to consider substantiated individual hardships. The court treated the compromise proposals as the base for resolving the dispute in light of the earlier remand and the representative proceedings conducted under Order 1 Rule 8 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908. It declined to decide the applicability of the Maharashtra Rent Control Act, 1999, without adequate pleadings and material.

predicates.appeal_over_public_authority_lease_rent_: The proceeding is an appeal concerning revision of rents by a public authority landlord.
predicates.representative_notice_given_to_affected_: Affected tenants were notified and given an opportunity to participate in representative proceedings concerning the common rent terms.
predicates.common_rent_terms_are_reasonable: The common rent terms are found fair and reasonable after considering the valuation basis and the parties’ positions.

issues.definition: In an appeal over a public landlord’s rent revision, reasonable common terms bind tenants covered by representative proceedings when those tenants were notified and given an opportunity to participate.

issues.legal_issue: A respondent cannot file cross-objections in a civil appeal brought by special leave, and a respondent seeking to challenge an adverse part of the decision must pursue an independent appeal in time.
material_facts: The trust filed cross-objections in the tenants’ appeals brought by special leave.
The trust had accepted and acted on the High Court judgment but sought through its cross-objections to restore its earlier position.
It had not filed an independent application for special leave within the applicable period, and the issue it sought to reopen had also been constrained by the earlier remand.
The trust’s challenge to the compromise proposals was also found to lack merit.
issues.conclusion: The cross-objections were dismissed as not maintainable and as devoid of merit.
issues.legal_principle: Order 41 Rule 22 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, does not create a right to file cross-objections in an appeal under Article 136 of the Constitution. Such objections are in substance an appeal, and a respondent aggrieved by an adverse part of a decision must seek leave to appeal independently. Article 136 confers discretionary, exceptional jurisdiction, not a statutory right of appeal. The court relied on Alopi Nath v. Collector, Varanasi; M/s Bengal Chemical & Pharmaceutical Works Ltd.; State of Bombay v. Rusy Mistry; Basudev Hazra; Arunachalam v. P.S.R. Sadanatham; Subedar v. State of U.P.; Pritam Singh v. State; Bharat Bank Ltd.; Vashist Narain Sharma v. Dev Chandra; and Sri Babu Ram v. Shrimati Prasanni.

predicates.special_leave_civil_appeal: The matter before the court is a civil appeal proceeding by special leave.
predicates.respondent_files_cross_objection: The respondent seeks to challenge the decision through a cross-objection rather than an independent appeal.
predicates.respondent_does_not_seek_timely_independ: The respondent does not seek independent appellate leave within the applicable time.

issues.definition: When a respondent in a civil appeal by special leave uses a cross-objection to challenge the decision without timely seeking independent appellate leave, the cross-objection is not maintainable.

issues.legal_issue: A respondent who has obtained a favorable order may support it on an alternative ground decided against the respondent below without filing a separate appeal or cross-objection.
material_facts: The trust relied on decisions in which respondents had been permitted to challenge adverse findings while supporting favorable final orders.
The court distinguished that situation from the trust’s cross-objections, which sought to challenge the decision itself and restore a less favorable result.
issues.conclusion: A respondent may support a favorable order by seeking reversal of an adverse finding on another ground, but that principle does not make cross-objections maintainable in an appeal by special leave.
issues.legal_principle: A party with an order in its favor may defend that order on an alternative ground decided against it below as a matter of general principles applicable to superior courts, not because Order 41 Rule 22 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, applies to appeals under Article 136. The court relied on Ramanbhai Ashabhai Patel, Management of Northern Railway Co-operative Society Ltd., Bharat Kala Bhandar Ltd., Nalakath Sainuddin v. Koorikadan Sulaiman, and Banarsi v. Ram Phal.

predicates.appeal_or_revision_before_superior_court: A superior court is hearing an appeal or revision concerning a lower court’s decision.
predicates.respondent_has_favorable_order: The respondent obtained a final order in its favor below.
predicates.respondent_seeks_only_to_support_that_or: The respondent seeks to preserve the favorable order by relying on a different ground, rather than to obtain a more favorable order.

issues.definition: A respondent with a favorable order may rely on an alternative ground to preserve that order when the respondent seeks no greater relief.

issues.legal_issue: A tenant claiming that material features of the leased property justify an exception to generally applicable rent terms may seek individual review through a designated adjudicator.
material_facts: The court found merit in the contention that some leased properties had distinguishing features that could justify a reduction in rent or another lease-term adjustment.
The tenant’s land was crossed along its length by an underground storm-water drain, restricting development, and the documentary material and valuation report supported that circumstance.
The court considered individual factual inquiries unsuitable for resolution in the general proceedings and established a procedure for written representations and summary adjudication.
issues.conclusion: A tenant could submit a timely representation identifying specific grounds and relevant facts, and a sole adjudicator appointed through the High Court was to decide whether that tenant was entitled to relief. The procedure did not permit withholding rent arrears pending the adjudicator’s decision.
issues.legal_principle: Common terms may govern a class of tenants while a tenant with real and material distinguishing features is given an opportunity to establish an individual entitlement to relief. The court directed summary consideration of representations, with the adjudicator able to receive documents or affidavits and inspect the property if appropriate.

predicates.public_authority_lease_rent_dispute: The proceeding concerns rents charged by a public authority landlord to its tenants.
predicates.general_rent_terms_apply: Common rent terms have been established for a group of tenants.
predicates.tenant_identifies_material_distinguishin: A tenant identifies specific features of the property or lease that may materially distinguish it from the properties or leases governed by the common terms.

issues.definition: Where common rent terms apply, a tenant who identifies material distinguishing features may seek individual relief.
